human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: MORSE presents a methodologically sound but incrementally novel framework for morpheme segmentation with credible contributions to dataset critique and empirical validation. The paper merits publication with revisions addressing critical methodological vulnerabilities. MAJOR CONCERNS (must address): (1) Arbitrary cosine threshold (0.1) lacks justification and sensitivity analysis—conduct sensitivity analysis varying threshold 0.0-0.5 and provide theoretical/empirical justification; (2) Vocabulary constraint (1M) confounds evaluation fairness—remove constraint or conduct controlled comparison with Morfessor using same vocabulary size; (3) Different tuning sets for MC vs. SD17 evaluation—report results with controlled tuning sets to isolate dataset effects; (4) SD17 dataset created by authors introduces potential bias—conduct independent validation or compare with other compositionality-based datasets; (5) Greedy inference acknowledged but impact not quantified—implement and compare alternative inference strategies. SECONDARY CONCERNS (should address): (1) No ablation studies isolating semantic feature contributions—conduct ablation studies; (2) Embedding quality degradation not empirically measured—measure embedding quality metrics across languages; (3) 'First' claim difficult to verify—conduct comprehensive literature search and clarify novelty claims; (4) Compositionality criterion not validated against downstream tasks—evaluate on IR, MT, ASR. CONFIDENCE IN ACCEPTANCE: Moderate-to-high (0.65-0.75) contingent on addressing major methodological issues. The work represents solid incremental progress in morpheme segmentation with useful dataset contributions, but claims of generality and necessity require stronger evidence. With revisions addressing major concerns, confidence increases to 0.75-0.85.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes credible contributions to morpheme segmentation and dataset evaluation, but several methodological choices require clarification or revision to strengthen validity of claims. CRITICAL REVISIONS NEEDED: (1) Cosine similarity threshold (0.1): Provide justification (empirical tuning on development set, theoretical motivation) and conduct sensitivity analysis showing F1 scores for thresholds 0.05-0.5. Investigate language-specific thresholds. (2) Vocabulary constraint (1M): Remove constraint and re-evaluate on Finnish, or conduct controlled comparison with Morfessor using same vocabulary size. Quantify impact on Finnish performance. (3) Evaluation confounds: Report three conditions: (a) both systems tuned on MC, evaluated on MC; (b) both systems tuned on SD17, evaluated on SD17; (c) both systems tuned on MC, evaluated on SD17. (4) SD17 dataset: Conduct independent annotation of subset by external annotators. Compare with other compositionality-based datasets. Analyze whether compositionality criterion systematically favors semantic methods. (5) Ablation studies: Isolate contribution of local vs. vocabulary-wide semantic features. Analyze which components contribute most to avoiding over-segmentation. (6) Greedy inference: Implement beam search or dynamic programming variant and compare performance. Quantify error propagation impact. IMPORTANT ADDITIONS: (7) Embedding quality: Measure word embedding quality in English, Turkish, Finnish using standard metrics (analogy task accuracy, nearest-neighbor accuracy). Correlate with MORSE performance. (8) Novelty claims: Conduct comprehensive literature search on difference-vector morpheme segmentation. Explicitly compare with Soricut & Och (2015). Revise 'first' claims if prior work exists. (9) Downstream evaluation: Evaluate MORSE and Morfessor on downstream tasks (IR, MT, ASR) to validate that compositionality-based segmentation improves real-world performance. (10) Non-compositional words: Expand test set to 500-1000 words with documented selection criteria. Report inter-annotator agreement. Provide breakdown by word type. These revisions will substantially strengthen validity of claims and address reviewer concerns about methodological rigor.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
MORSE proposes integrating vocabulary-wide semantic validation (via word embedding difference vectors) with orthographic features for morpheme segmentation. The paper makes six primary claims: (1) first to leverage vocabulary-wide syntactico-semantic information; (2) difference-vector consistency validates affix rules at corpus scale; (3) Morpho Challenge datasets violate compositionality and contain trivial instances; (4) semantic information is necessary to avoid over-segmentation of non-compositional words; (5) MORSE achieves state-of-the-art on English/Turkish but degrades on morphologically rich languages; (6) compositionality-driven evaluation reveals 24% F1 improvement vs. 6% on standard benchmarks. The paper makes credible incremental contributions with empirical validation across three languages, but multiple methodological vulnerabilities limit confidence in core claims.

Strengths:
- Novel multi-level semantic validation framework combining local and vocabulary-wide difference-vector consistency checking; represents meaningful extension of prior local semantic methods (Narasimhan et al. 2015)
- Substantive critical analysis of Morpho Challenge dataset deficiencies with concrete examples (non-compositional segmentations, trivial instances); linguistically grounded and contributes to understanding of evaluation methodology
- Compositionality-driven dataset (SD17) with 91% inter-annotator agreement provides valuable alternative evaluation framework; publicly released
- Empirical validation across three typologically diverse languages (English, Turkish, Finnish) with varying morphological richness; reveals language-dependent performance patterns
- Practical demonstration of semantic method's robustness to non-compositional words: 7 false morphemes (MORSE) vs. 43 (Morfessor) on 100-word test set
- Minimal supervision requirement (~300 gold segmentations) is practical advantage; reaches steady-state performance at 20% of tuning data
- Clear algorithmic formalization with explicit definitions; source code and datasets released publicly supporting reproducibility
- Transparent acknowledgment of limitations (greedy inference, concatenative morphology only, vocabulary constraints, Finnish performance degradation) prevents overclaiming

Limitations:
- Cosine similarity threshold (0.1) for difference-vector consistency appears arbitrary with no justification, sensitivity analysis, or language-specific tuning. This critical hyperparameter directly affects which affix rules are validated, but its appropriateness is not validated across languages or morpheme types. Results may be sensitive to this choice.
- Vocabulary constraint (1M) is implementation choice that unfairly disadvantages MORSE on morphologically rich languages. Finnish performance substantially degrades (14.98% vs. 34.06% Morfessor), but unclear whether this reflects semantic approach limitations or vocabulary constraint. No controlled comparison with Morfessor using same vocabulary size provided. This confounds evaluation of the semantic approach itself.
- Evaluation confounded by different tuning sets: MORSE tuned on MC for standard evaluation (Table 3) but cross-validated on SD17 for SD17 evaluation (Table 5). The 24% improvement on SD17 vs. 6% on MC may reflect better hyperparameter tuning for SD17 rather than dataset differences. No report of MC-tuned MORSE performance on SD17 for fair comparison.
- SD17 dataset created by authors introduces potential annotation bias toward semantic methods. Compositionality criterion may inherently favor semantic approaches. No independent validation beyond 91% inter-annotator agreement; no comparison with other compositionality-based datasets. Claim that MC 'underestimates' semantic methods assumes SD17 is ground truth.
- Greedy sequential inference acknowledged as limitation but impact not quantified. Early incorrect segmentation decisions propagate to later decisions, but no comparison with global optimization or beam search provided. Performance ceiling with alternative inference strategies unknown.
- No ablation studies isolating contribution of local vs. vocabulary-wide semantic features. Both components used together without analysis of relative importance. Unclear which semantic features contribute most to avoiding over-segmentation of non-compositional words.

Open Questions:
- What is the sensitivity of MORSE performance to the cosine similarity threshold (0.1)? How does performance vary with thresholds from 0.0 to 0.5? Should language-specific or morpheme-type-specific thresholds be used? What theoretical or empirical justification supports the choice of 0.1?
- How much of the Finnish performance degradation (14.98% vs. 34.06% Morfessor) is due to the vocabulary constraint (1M) vs. fundamental limitations of the semantic approach? What is MORSE performance on Finnish with larger vocabulary (5M, 10M)? How does Morfessor perform with same vocabulary constraint?
- Is the 24% improvement on SD17 vs. 6% on MC due to dataset differences or hyperparameter tuning differences? What is MORSE performance on SD17 using MC-tuned hyperparameters? What is Morfessor-CV performance on SD17 using same cross-validation procedure?
- Does SD17 dataset introduce bias toward semantic methods? How do results compare with other compositionality-based morpheme segmentation datasets? Do non-semantic baselines (e.g., frequency-based filtering) also improve on SD17 compared to MC?
- What is the impact of greedy sequential inference on performance? How much does beam search or dynamic programming improve results? How frequently does error propagation occur (early incorrect segmentation leading to downstream errors)?

Transparency:
- This meta-review synthesizes five specialist reviewers with distinct cognitive roles to provide comprehensive analysis from multiple epistemic perspectives
- Consensus findings reflect agreement across multiple reviewers on core methodological issues (arbitrary threshold, vocabulary constraint, evaluation confounds, insufficient ablation studies); these are well-evidenced and consistently identified
- Disagreements primarily concern interpretation of sparse prior art and causal attribution of Finnish performance degradation; reviewers agree on existence of issues but differ on whether they reflect fundamental limitations vs. implementation constraints
- Model diversity reveals that different cognitive roles identify consistent vulnerabilities, suggesting these are genuine methodological issues rather than role-specific concerns
- Uncertainty hotspots explicitly identified with actionable suggestions for resolution; confidence intervals reflect uncertainty in verification
- Paper's strengths (novel semantic validation framework, critical analysis of MC dataset, SD17 dataset, multi-language evaluation) consistently recognized across reviewers; concerns focus on methodological rigor rather than conceptual validity
- Epistemic limits explicitly identified: verification of 'first' claim requires comprehensive literature search; causal attribution of Finnish performance degradation limited by lack of controlled experiments; compositionality criterion validity cannot be assessed without downstream task evaluation; embedding quality degradation hypothesized but not empirically measured
- Meta-review preserves controlled disagreement rather than averaging opinions into flat verdict; editor retains central decision role with clear guidance on major vs. secondary concerns

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence interval reflects evidence-and-uncertainty-first epistemic stance. Lower bound (0.55) reflects major methodological concerns: arbitrary cosine threshold (0.1) lacks justification, vocabulary constraint (1M) confounds evaluation fairness, different tuning sets (MC vs. SD17) confound improvement claims, and author-created SD17 dataset introduces potential bias. These issues are well-evidenced and actionable. Upper bound (0.75) reflects genuine contributions: novel multi-level semantic validation framework, substantive critique of MC dataset deficiencies, compositionality-driven dataset (SD17) with reasonable inter-annotator agreement (91%), and empirical validation across three languages. The paper makes credible incremental advances but with significant methodological limitations that affect validity of main claims. Confidence would increase to 0.75-0.85 if: (1) cosine threshold is justified and sensitivity-analyzed; (2) vocabulary constraint is removed and Finnish re-evaluated; (3) evaluation is controlled with same tuning sets; (4) SD17 is independently validated. Confidence would decrease to 0.40-0.55 if: (1) 'first' claim cannot be verified; (2) Finnish failure is shown to be fundamental limitation of semantic approach; (3) 24% improvement is shown to reflect dataset bias rather than methodological superiority.

Our work also relates to the log-linear model for morphological segmentation developed by Poon et al. (2009). They propose a joint model over all words (observations) and their segmentations (hid- den), using morphemes and their contexts (charac- ter n-grams) for the features. Since the space of all possible segmentation sets is huge, learning and in- ference are quite involved. They use techniques like Contrastive Estimation, sampling and simulated an- nealing. In contrast, our formulation does not re- sult in such a large search space. For each word, the number of parent candidates is bounded by its length multiplied by the number of possible trans- formations. Therefore, Contrastive Estimation can be implemented via enumeration, and does not re- quire sampling. top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: Most state-of-the-art unsupervised approaches to morphological analysis are built primarily around orthographic patterns in morphologically-related words (Goldwater and Johnson, 2004; Creutz and Lagus, 2007; Snyder and Barzilay, 2008; Poon et al., 2009). In these approaches, words are com- monly modeled as concatenations of morphemes. 1Code is available at https://github.com/ karthikncode/MorphoChain. This morpheme-centric view is well-suited for un- covering distributional properties of stems and af- ﬁxes. But it is not well-equipped to capture semantic relatedness at the word level. In contrast, earlier approaches that capture se- mantic similarity in morphological variants oper- ate solely at the word level (Schone and Juraf- sky, 2000; Baroni et al., 2002). Given two candi- date words, the proximity is assessed using standard word-distributional measures such as mutual infor- mation. However, the fact that these models do not model morphemes directly greatly limits their per- formance. In this paper, we propose a model to integrate or- thographic and semantic views. Our goal is to build a chain of derivations for a current word from its base form. For instance, given a word playfully, the corresponding chain is play→playful→playfully. The word play is a base form of this derivation as it cannot be reduced any further. Individual deriva- tions are obtained by adding a morpheme (ex. -ful) to a parent word (ex. play). Working on the level of characters alleviates this problem to a large extent, as the vocabulary of possible characters is much smaller than the vocabulary of possible words. However, working on the character level is very challenging, as the relationship between form (characters) and function (syntax, semantics) in language is quite loose. Restricting oneself to stay on the character level may be an unnecessarily hard constraint. Some researchers propose a middle-ground, in which a word is represented as a combination of a vector for the word itself with vectors of sub-word units that comprise it. The sub-word embeddings then help in sharing information between diﬀerent words with similar forms, as well as allowing back-oﬀ to the subword level when the word is not observed. At the same time, the models are not forced to rely solely on form when enough observations of the word are available. top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: Most state-of-the-art unsupervised approaches to morphological analysis are built primarily around orthographic patterns in morphologically-related words (Goldwater and Johnson, 2004; Creutz and Lagus, 2007; Snyder and Barzilay, 2008; Poon et al., 2009). In these approaches, words are com- monly modeled as concatenations of morphemes. 1Code is available at https://github.com/ karthikncode/MorphoChain. This morpheme-centric view is well-suited for un- covering distributional properties of stems and af- ﬁxes. But it is not well-equipped to capture semantic relatedness at the word level. In contrast, earlier approaches that capture se- mantic similarity in morphological variants oper- ate solely at the word level (Schone and Juraf- sky, 2000; Baroni et al., 2002). Given two candi- date words, the proximity is assessed using standard word-distributional measures such as mutual infor- mation. However, the fact that these models do not model morphemes directly greatly limits their per- formance. In this paper, we propose a model to integrate or- thographic and semantic views. Our goal is to build a chain of derivations for a current word from its base form. For instance, given a word playfully, the corresponding chain is play→playful→playfully. The word play is a base form of this derivation as it cannot be reduced any further. Individual deriva- tions are obtained by adding a morpheme (ex. -ful) to a parent word (ex. play). Working on the level of characters alleviates this problem to a large extent, as the vocabulary of possible characters is much smaller than the vocabulary of possible words. However, working on the character level is very challenging, as the relationship between form (characters) and function (syntax, semantics) in language is quite loose. Restricting oneself to stay on the character level may be an unnecessarily hard constraint. Some researchers propose a middle-ground, in which a word is represented as a combination of a vector for the word itself with vectors of sub-word units that comprise it. The sub-word embeddings then help in sharing information between diﬀerent words with similar forms, as well as allowing back-oﬀ to the subword level when the word is not observed. At the same time, the models are not forced to rely solely on form when enough observations of the word are available. Using EMMA we can evaluate the induced segmentations of German words against gold standard analyses. EMMA has a freely available implementation,9 but is slow to compute because it uses Integer Linear Programming. For our dev results, we computed both scores us- ing the entire dev set, but for the large test sets, the evaluation is done on batches of 1000 word types se- lected randomly from the test set. This procedure is repeated 10 times and the average is reported, just as in the MC2010 competition (Kohonen et al., 2010a). 4.3 Baseline Models We compare our AG models to several other mor- phology learning systems. Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Working on the level of characters alleviates this problem to a large extent, as the vocabulary of possible characters is much smaller than the vocabulary of possible words. However, working on the character level is very challenging, as the relationship between form (characters) and function (syntax, semantics) in language is quite loose. Restricting oneself to stay on the character level may be an unnecessarily hard constraint. Some researchers propose a middle-ground, in which a word is represented as a combination of a vector for the word itself with vectors of sub-word units that comprise it. The sub-word embeddings then help in sharing information between diﬀerent words with similar forms, as well as allowing back-oﬀ to the subword level when the word is not observed. At the same time, the models are not forced to rely solely on form when enough observations of the word are available. Our work also relates to the log-linear model for morphological segmentation developed by Poon et al. (2009). They propose a joint model over all words (observations) and their segmentations (hid- den), using morphemes and their contexts (charac- ter n-grams) for the features. In contrast, our formulation does not re- sult in such a large search space. For each word, the number of parent candidates is bounded by its length multiplied by the number of possible trans- formations. top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: Most state-of-the-art unsupervised approaches to morphological analysis are built primarily around orthographic patterns in morphologically-related words (Goldwater and Johnson, 2004; Creutz and Lagus, 2007; Snyder and Barzilay, 2008; Poon et al., 2009). In these approaches, words are com- monly modeled as concatenations of morphemes. 1Code is available at https://github.com/ karthikncode/MorphoChain. This morpheme-centric view is well-suited for un- covering distributional properties of stems and af- ﬁxes. But it is not well-equipped to capture semantic relatedness at the word level. In contrast, earlier approaches that capture se- mantic similarity in morphological variants oper- ate solely at the word level (Schone and Juraf- sky, 2000; Baroni et al., 2002). Given two candi- date words, the proximity is assessed using standard word-distributional measures such as mutual infor- mation. However, the fact that these models do not model morphemes directly greatly limits their per- formance. In this paper, we propose a model to integrate or- thographic and semantic views. Our goal is to build a chain of derivations for a current word from its base form. For instance, given a word playfully, the corresponding chain is play→playful→playfully. While the contribu- tion varies from 3% on Turkish to 11% on the En- glish dataset, it nevertheless improves performance across all the languages. 2 Related Work Currently, top performing unsupervised morpholog- ical analyzers are based on the orthographic prop- erties of sub-word units (Creutz and Lagus, 2005; Creutz and Lagus, 2007; Poon et al., 2009; Sirts and Goldwater, 2013). Adding semantic information to these systems is not an easy task, as they operate at the level of individual morphemes, rather than mor- phologically related words. The value of semantic information has been demonstrated in earlier work on morphological anal- ysis. Schone and Jurafsky (2000) employ an LSA- based similarity measure to identify morphological variants from a list of orthographically close word pairs. The ﬁltered pairs are then used to identify stems and afﬁxes. Based on similar intuition, Baroni et al. (2002) design a method that integrates these sources of information, captured as two word pair lists, ranked based on edit distance and mutual in- formation. These lists are subsequently combined using a deterministic weighting function. In both of these algorithms, orthographic related- ness is based on simple deterministic rules. Four versions of the system were evaluated in MC2010, using differ- ent degrees of supervision. Results reported here are from the Morfessor S+W system, which performed best of those that use the same kind of labelled data as we do. 11 This system uses the Morfessor Base- line model (not Cat-MAP), which incorporates a lexicon prior and data likelihood term. Content: n doubt, consider the scope described in ARR CFP and any relevant conferences (e.g. for October 2024 cycle the NAACL CFP specifies the special theme “NLP in a Multicultural World”. Hallucinated references or citations: Please check carefully for hallucinated references, which pose a serious concern to scientific reliability. Anonymity violations. As of January 2024, non-anonymous pre-prints are permitted for ARR, but submissions should still be properly anonymized (e.g., not containing explicit references to the authors’ prior work, acknowledgements, links to non-anonymous repositories or services like Dropbox that may track who opened the link). Style guides or length violations: the paper should be desk-rejected if it does not follow the style guides or goes over the page limit (4 pages for short, 8 for long papers, excluding the ethical considerations and limitations).

Section: 🆕 4. Check for common problems in NLP papers
Codes: M1, G2
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor
Content: As a counter to common problems with reviews, there are also common problems with NLP papers. We do ask you to watch out for these and point them out when you see them. Above all else, published research should at least be technically sound and appropriately scoped. As with the above reviewer issues, it’s a case-by-case evaluation: some things in the list below may be appropriate in a given context, given that they are sufficiently motivated. We provide codes for different types of issues (e.g. M1, G2…) that can be referenced in discussions.
